hub_tagline: Four words for the four pieces of one computation step, placed side by side and on one picture, with the mix-ups named and corrected.

concepts.title: Concept: Redex
concepts.tagline: The sub-term about to be rewritten: a rule's left side, found somewhere inside a term.
concepts.sentence: A redex is a sub-term matching a rule's left side: (λx. M) N for β, or λx. M x (x ∉ FV(M)) for η. It's the before of one step.
concepts.analogy_big: The redex is the sealed envelope you're about to open.
concepts.analogy: It's still in the pile, exactly as written. Nothing has happened to it yet.
concepts.see:
(λx. x x) ([(λy. y) z])
  context    C[□] = (λx. x x) □
  redex           = (λy. y) z
  contractum      = z
  reduct  C[…]    = (λx. x x) z

Real npm run demo output for one step.
concepts.wrong: "The redex is the whole term being reduced."
concepts.right: The redex is the one sub-term that gets rewritten. The whole term is context + redex. Here, the whole term is (λx. x x) ((λy. y) z) and the redex is only (λy. y) z.
concepts.connects: A redex sits inside a context. Contracting it gives the contractum. Putting that back into the context gives the reduct.

concepts.title: Concept: Contractum
concepts.tagline: What a redex turns into: the rule's right side, e.g. M[x := N] for β.
concepts.sentence: The contractum is the result of applying the rule to the redex alone: (λx. M) N ↦ M[x := N]. It replaces the redex and nothing else.
concepts.analogy_big: The contractum is the envelope's contents with the letter already dropped in.
concepts.analogy: It's local. It knows nothing about the rest of the pile.
concepts.see:
λz. [(λx. λz. x z) z]
  context    C[□] = λz. □
  redex           = (λx. λz. x z) z
  contractum      = λz1. z z1   (renamed z→z1 to avoid capture)
  reduct  C[…]    = λz. λz1. z z1

Real demo output. Module 5's capture avoidance happens right here, while building the contractum.
concepts.wrong: "The contractum is the new term after the step."
concepts.right: That's the reduct. The contractum only replaces the redex. For (λx. x x) ((λy. y) z) stepping inside, the contractum is z but the new term is (λx. x x) z.
concepts.connects: Contracting a redex gives the contractum. Plugging it into the same context gives the reduct.

concepts.title: Concept: Context
concepts.tagline: The whole term with a hole where the redex sits. It records where the step happens.
concepts.sentence: A context C[□] is a term with exactly one hole. C[R] fills the hole with R. Every one-step reduction has the form C[R] → C[R'].
concepts.analogy_big: The context is the pile of papers with one envelope-shaped gap.
concepts.analogy: Lift the envelope out, open it, and put the result back in the same gap. The rest of the pile never changes.
concepts.see:
λx. [(λy. y) x] z
  context    C[□] = λx. □ z
  rules used      : ξ ∘ app-L ∘ β

In the engine, a context is data with one constructor per congruence rule (appL, appR, lam for ξ), so its shape is the chain of inference rules the step uses.
concepts.wrong: "Filling a context's hole is substitution, so it must avoid capture."
concepts.right: Plugging is deliberately not capture-avoiding. Filling λx. □ with x gives λx. x, because a redex under a λ must see that λ's variable. Substitution replaces free variables; plugging fills a hole.
concepts.connects: The context surrounds the redex. Swapping the redex for its contractum inside the same context produces the reduct.

concepts.title: Concept: Reduct
concepts.tagline: The whole term after the step: the context with the contractum plugged into its hole.
concepts.sentence: If M → N, then N is a (one-step) reduct of M: M = C[redex] and N = C[contractum]. With →*, "a reduct" means anything reachable in zero or more steps.
concepts.analogy_big: The reduct is the whole pile after you've opened one envelope.
concepts.analogy: Only one spot changed. Everything else is exactly as it was.
concepts.see:
(λx. x x) ((λy. y) z)  →β  (λy. y) z ((λy. y) z)      (redex at ε)
(λx. x x) ((λy. y) z)  →β  (λx. x x) z      (redex at arg)

Real demo output. A term has one one-step reduct per redex.
concepts.wrong: "A term's reduct is its normal form."
concepts.right: A reduct is just somewhere further along, and a term can have many. The normal form, if there is one, is the special reduct with no redexes left.
concepts.connects: The reduct is the context with the contractum where the redex used to be.

picture_caption: One step: C[redex] → C[contractum], and the result is the reduct.
pairs: The contractum replaces only the redex (z). The reduct is the whole new term ((λx. x x) z).
"This term is a redex, so it reduces."
A term can contain redexes without being one: f ((λx. x) y).
"Plugging a hole avoids capture, like substitution."
Plugging must capture: λx. □ filled with x is λx. x.
A reduct is one step on. The normal form is the reduct (if any) with no redexes left.
quiz: In one step of (λa. a a) b, the part (λa. a a) b.
It matches (λx. M) N. Here the redex happens to be the whole term.
For that step, the local result b b.
The rule's right side. Since the context is just □, the reduct is also b b.
For a step inside λq. (λa. a) q, the thing written λq. □.
Everything except the redex, with a hole.
For that same step, the whole result λq. q.
The context with the contractum q plugged in.
In f ((λx. x) y) → f y, the y that replaced (λx. x) y.
In f ((λx. x) y) → f y, the whole f y.
